definition: Synchronous context-free grammars (SynCFG or SCFG; not to be confused with stochastic CFGs) are a type of formal grammar designed for use in transfer-based machine translation.
details: Rules in these grammars apply to two languages at the same time, capturing grammatical structures that are each other's translations. The theory of SynCFGs borrows from syntax-directed transduction and syntax-based machine translation, modeling the reordering of clauses that occurs when translating a sentence by correspondences between phrase-structure rules in the source and target languages. Performance of SCFG-based MT systems has been found comparable with, or even better than, state-of-the-art phrase-based machine translation systems. Several algorithms exist to perform translation using SynCFGs.

explainer.lead: Synchronous context-free grammars pair rewrite rules across two languages at once, making them a workhorse for transfer-based machine translation. They matter because they encode how source structure maps to target structure, including reordering.

tiers.eli5: Think of two matching sets of building instructions, one in each language, that must be applied in step so the same sentence gets built twice.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers write paired phrase-structure rules so each parse in the source yields an aligned target; a common pitfall is rule explosion, where coverage demands so many rules that decoding and maintenance become unwieldy.
tiers.paperLevel: A rule has a source side and target side with correspondences between nonterminals, applied in tandem to derive both sides simultaneously; the formalism cannot capture unbounded dependencies that lie outside context-free phrase structure.

explainer.example: A rule pairing an English verb-object phrase with a Japanese object-verb phrase forces the object to precede the verb in the target while keeping the same words aligned.
